title: repayDebt and reduceCredit declared as public in a library — callable by anyone
description: Both `repayDebt` (line 44) and `reduceCredit` (line 128) are declared `public` in a Solidity library. In Solidity 0.8.x, `public` library functions are deployed as part of the library's external interface, meaning they can be called directly by any external account against the deployed library contract. Since these functions take a `State storage` pointer, an external caller that obtains the correct storage slot layout could manipulate the state directly — burning debt tokens from arbitrary borrowers, reducing future values, and reducing credit positions without authorization. Even if the library is used with `delegatecall` (the normal use case), the functions being `public` instead of `internal` means the linker exposes them as external entry points on the library itself.
message: An attacker can call `repayDebt` directly on the library contract to burn debt tokens from any borrower without transferring any repayment funds, effectively wiping debt balances. Similarly, `reduceCredit` can be called to reduce lender credit positions to zero, causing lenders to lose their owed funds. This can drain the protocol's accounting state entirely.
exploit_scenario: 1. Deploy the protocol normally; the AccountingLibrary is deployed as a standalone library contract. 2. Attacker identifies the library's deployed address. 3. Attacker calls `AccountingLibrary.repayDebt(state, victimDebtPositionId, fullFutureValue)` directly on the library address, passing in a crafted `state` storage reference. 4. The debt is burned without any actual repayment. 5. Attacker calls `reduceCredit(state, creditPositionId, fullCreditAmount)` to zero out lender credit. 6. Borrower keeps collateral; lenders lose their claims.

title: createDebtAndCreditPositions declared external in a library — callable externally without authorization
description: `createDebtAndCreditPositions` is declared `external` in the library. This exposes it as a callable external function on the deployed library contract. An attacker can call this function directly on the library, passing arbitrary `lender`, `borrower`, `futureValue`, and `dueDate` parameters. This mints debt tokens to any borrower address without requiring any collateral check, bypassing all the lending protocol's safety checks (LTV validation, collateral requirements, etc.).
message: Attacker can mint unlimited debt tokens to any address by calling the library directly, bypassing all collateral and LTV checks. This inflates the debt token supply and can be used to drain the protocol if debt tokens have any redemption value, or to manipulate protocol accounting.
exploit_scenario: 1. Locate the deployed AccountingLibrary contract address. 2. Call `createDebtAndCreditPositions(state, attackerAddress, attackerAddress, 1e30, futureTimestamp)` directly on the library. 3. The library mints `1e30` debt tokens to the attacker's address. 4. Debt positions and credit positions are created without any collateral being locked. 5. Attacker uses inflated positions to claim assets or manipulate the protocol.

title: createCreditPosition declared external in a library — unauthorized credit position creation
description: `createCreditPosition` is declared `external` in the library, making it callable by any external account against the library contract. This function can reassign credit position lenders or create new credit positions with arbitrary credit amounts by calling `reduceCredit` on existing positions. An attacker could redirect credit owed to legitimate lenders to themselves, or create ghost credit positions.
message: Attacker can steal credit positions from legitimate lenders by reassigning them, or create new credit positions pointing to existing debt positions with arbitrary credit amounts, breaking the invariant that the sum of credit positions equals the debt position future value.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker identifies a creditPositionId belonging to a victim lender. 2. Attacker calls `createCreditPosition(state, victimCreditPositionId, attackerAddress, victimCreditAmount)` directly on the library. 3. Since `credit == exitCreditPosition.credit`, the lender field is updated to the attacker's address. 4. When the debt is repaid, the attacker claims the funds instead of the legitimate lender.

title: Division by zero in getCreditAmountIn when swapFeePercent equals PERCENT
message: If a malicious or misconfigured fee APR and tenor combination causes `swapFeePercent >= PERCENT`, all credit-fractionalization buy orders will permanently revert, effectively DoS-ing that code path. Additionally, if governance sets an extreme fee APR, the protocol becomes unusable.
exploit_scenario: 1. Set `swapFeeAPR` to a high value such that for a 1-year tenor, `getSwapFeePercent` returns >= PERCENT. 2. Any call to `getCreditAmountIn` with `cashAmountOut < maxCashAmountOutFragmentation` will hit division by zero or underflow. 3. All credit-fractionalized buys revert.

title: Missing minimum credit validation after reduceCredit in createCreditPosition for full-credit transfer case
description: In `createCreditPosition`, when `exitCreditPosition.credit == credit` (full credit transfer), only the lender is updated — no `validateMinimumCreditOpening` or `validateMinimumCredit` is called on the exit position. More critically, the `reduceCredit` path (when `credit < exitCreditPosition.credit`) calls `validateMinimumCredit` on the exit position after reduction (inside `reduceCredit`), but the invariant check is that the remaining credit in `exitCreditPosition` must meet the minimum. If `reduceCredit` leaves `exitCreditPosition.credit` at exactly 0 (which would only happen if `credit == exitCreditPosition.credit` but that branch takes the other path), or near-zero values pass the minimum check, dust positions can persist. However, the more serious issue is that `validateMinimumCredit` in `reduceCredit` may allow the exit position's credit to go to 0 if `validateMinimumCredit` permits 0 (dust position). This breaks the accounting invariant where the sum of credit positions should equal the debt future value.
message: Dust credit positions can accumulate, breaking the invariant that total credit equals total debt. This can prevent borrowers from fully repaying debt or cause lenders to be unable to claim their full owed amount.
recommendation: Ensure `validateMinimumCredit` strictly rejects 0-value credits, and ensure the new credit position in the fractionalization path also satisfies `validateMinimumCreditOpening`. Review whether a credit position reduced to 0 should be deleted from the mapping rather than persisted as a dust entry.
exploit_scenario: 1. Create a debt+credit position with futureValue = minimumCredit + 1. 2. Call `createCreditPosition` with `credit = 1` (below minimum but passing `validateMinimumCredit` if it allows 0). 3. Exit position credit becomes `minimumCredit`, new position has credit 1. 4. The new position with credit 1 passes `validateMinimumCreditOpening` only if minimum is 0. 5. Dust positions accumulate.

title: Unconstrained swapFeeAPR, fragmentationFee, and liquidationRewardPercent Allow Griefing/Fund Drain
description: The validation function explicitly marks swapFeeAPR, fragmentationFee, and liquidationRewardPercent as 'N/A' with no upper bound checks. A misconfigured or malicious deployment could set swapFeeAPR to an extremely large value (e.g., type(uint256).max), causing overflow or near-100% fee extraction in swap fee calculations elsewhere in the protocol. Similarly, liquidationRewardPercent has no cap — if set above PERCENT (100%), liquidators could claim more collateral than the protocol holds, enabling fund drainage during liquidations.
message: If liquidationRewardPercent > PERCENT, liquidators receive more collateral than the debt they repay, effectively draining protocol collateral. If swapFeeAPR is set to type(uint256).max, any fee calculation using it will overflow (in unchecked contexts) or revert, bricking the protocol.
recommendation: Add explicit upper bound validation for all fee parameters: require liquidationRewardPercent <= PERCENT, require swapFeeAPR <= some reasonable maximum (e.g., 1e18 or PERCENT), require fragmentationFee <= some reasonable maximum. Example: if (f.liquidationRewardPercent > PERCENT) revert Errors.INVALID_COLLATERAL_PERCENTAGE_PREMIUM(f.liquidationRewardPercent);
exploit_scenario: 1. Deploy protocol with liquidationRewardPercent = type(uint256).max (no validation rejects this). 2. A borrower opens a position. 3. When position becomes liquidatable, liquidator calls liquidate(). 4. Protocol calculates liquidation reward as collateral * liquidationRewardPercent / PERCENT, which overflows or returns an astronomically large value. 5. If overflow doesn't revert, liquidator drains all collateral from the protocol.

title: WETH Address Not Validated — Zero Address or Malicious Contract Accepted
description: The validateInitializeDataParams function validates underlyingCollateralToken, underlyingBorrowToken, and variablePool addresses for zero-address and decimal constraints, but completely omits validation of the weth address (d.weth). A zero address or malicious contract set as WETH would cause all ETH-related operations (wrapping/unwrapping) to fail or behave unexpectedly, potentially locking user ETH in the contract permanently.
message: If weth is set to address(0) or a malicious contract: (1) All ETH deposit operations that call weth.deposit() will revert or call into attacker-controlled code, (2) ETH sent to the protocol cannot be wrapped/unwrapped, permanently locking funds, (3) A malicious WETH contract could reenter the protocol during deposit/withdrawal flows.
recommendation: Add WETH address validation in validateInitializeDataParams: if (d.weth == address(0)) revert Errors.NULL_ADDRESS(); Additionally, verify it's a valid WETH contract by checking decimals or calling a known interface method.
exploit_scenario: 1. Initialize protocol with d.weth = address(0) (passes all validation). 2. User calls depositETH() which internally calls state.data.weth.deposit{value: amount}(). 3. Call to address(0) succeeds silently (ETH is burned) or reverts, depending on implementation. 4. User's ETH is permanently lost.

title: borrowATokenCap Can Be Zero — Effectively Disables All Borrowing
description: The comment in validateInitializeRiskConfigParams explicitly marks borrowATokenCap validation as 'N/A'. A borrowATokenCap of 0 means no borrowing is ever allowed (since any borrow amount > 0 would exceed the cap), effectively bricking the protocol's core functionality. While this could be a misconfiguration rather than an exploit, it has no recovery path without an upgrade if initialization cannot be re-run.
message: Protocol is deployed with borrowATokenCap = 0, making it impossible for any user to borrow. All lender funds are permanently locked with no way to earn yield. Protocol is completely non-functional.
recommendation: Add validation: if (r.borrowATokenCap == 0) revert Errors.NULL_AMOUNT(); or at minimum enforce a minimum meaningful cap value.
exploit_scenario: 1. Deploy with r.borrowATokenCap = 0. 2. User attempts to borrow any amount. 3. Check `totalBorrowAToken + amount <= borrowATokenCap` fails (0 >= any positive amount). 4. All borrow operations revert permanently.

title: msg.value Reuse in Payable Multicall Allows ETH Accounting Manipulation
description: The `multicall` function is marked `payable` and calls `state.multicall(_data)` which internally executes multiple sub-calls (including `deposit`) using `delegatecall` or direct calls. Since `msg.value` remains constant throughout the entire multicall execution, any sub-call that credits ETH based on `msg.value` can be triggered multiple times within a single transaction, each time 'seeing' the full `msg.value`. If `deposit` uses `msg.value` to credit the user with ETH/WETH, a user can call multicall with N deposit operations and only send ETH once, being credited N times the actual ETH sent. This is the classic 'msg.value in loop' vulnerability.
message: An attacker can deposit ETH once but receive credit for N times that amount by including N deposit calls in the multicall array. This allows draining the protocol's ETH/WETH reserves or minting unbacked credit positions.
recommendation: Either (1) remove `payable` from multicall and require all ETH handling to use WETH explicitly, or (2) track how much msg.value has been consumed and prevent reuse: use a transient storage variable that tracks remaining ETH and subtract from it each time it's used in a deposit. The safest fix is to make multicall non-payable and force users to wrap ETH before depositing.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker calls multicall([deposit(ETH, amount), deposit(ETH, amount), deposit(ETH, amount)]) with msg.value = amount. 2. Each deposit call reads msg.value = amount and credits the attacker. 3. Attacker is credited 3*amount but only sent amount. 4. Attacker withdraws 3*amount, stealing 2*amount from other depositors.

title: No Bounds Validation on setVariablePoolBorrowRate Allows Oracle Manipulation
description: The `setVariablePoolBorrowRate` function accepts any `uint128` value without bounds checking. The `BORROW_RATE_UPDATER_ROLE` can set the variable pool borrow rate to an arbitrarily large or small value (including 0 or type(uint128).max). This rate likely feeds into interest calculations, loan valuations, and potentially liquidation thresholds. If the rate is set to an extreme value (either 0 or max), it could: (1) make all loans appear healthy or unhealthy, (2) manipulate the cost of borrowing to near-zero enabling excessive leverage, (3) cause interest calculation overflows or underflows in dependent math.
message: A compromised or malicious BORROW_RATE_UPDATER_ROLE can set the rate to 0 (enabling free borrowing with no interest costs, draining the protocol) or to max (making all borrowers instantly underwater and liquidatable). If this role is an EOA or less-secure multisig, it represents a significant centralization risk with direct fund loss potential.
recommendation: Add bounds checking: require the new rate to be within a reasonable range (e.g., between a MIN_BORROW_RATE and MAX_BORROW_RATE constant). Also consider adding a maximum rate-of-change check per time period (e.g., rate cannot change by more than X% per hour) to prevent sudden large manipulations.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker compromises BORROW_RATE_UPDATER_ROLE key. 2. Calls setVariablePoolBorrowRate(0) to set borrow rate to 0. 3. Users borrow at 0% interest indefinitely. 4. OR: calls setVariablePoolBorrowRate(type(uint128).max). 5. All borrowers become underwater due to extreme interest accrual. 6. Attacker liquidates all positions at extreme discount.

title: Missing Reentrancy Guard on Critical State-Changing Functions
description: None of the state-changing functions in Size.sol have a reentrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin's `nonReentrant` modifier). The contract interacts with external tokens (transferring ETH, ERC20 tokens) during deposit, withdraw, liquidate, and repay operations. If any of the tokens involved (collateral token, borrow token) are ERC777 tokens or tokens with hooks (transfer callbacks), a malicious token contract could reenter Size during a state-changing operation before state is fully updated. Additionally, the multicall function allows arbitrary sequences of operations, which combined with reentrancy could lead to inconsistent state.
message: An attacker using a token with transfer hooks could reenter the contract mid-operation when state is partially updated. For example, during a liquidation that transfers collateral to the liquidator, if the collateral token has a hook, the attacker could reenter and call liquidate again on the same position before it's marked as liquidated, double-claiming the collateral.
recommendation: Add OpenZeppelin's `ReentrancyGuardUpgradeable` to the contract inheritance and apply `nonReentrant` modifier to all state-changing external functions: deposit, withdraw, buyCreditMarket, sellCreditMarket, repay, claim, liquidate, selfLiquidate, liquidateWithReplacement, compensate, setUserConfiguration.
exploit_scenario: 1. Deploy malicious ERC777-compatible collateral token with a receive hook. 2. Create a position using this token as collateral. 3. Trigger liquidation. 4. During collateral transfer to liquidator, the token's hook calls back into liquidate() or selfLiquidate(). 5. The position may not be fully cleared yet, allowing double-liquidation. 6. Extract double the collateral value.

title: buyCreditMarket Validates Borrower CR Instead of Caller CR
description: In `buyCreditMarket`, when `params.creditPositionId == RESERVED_ID` (new loan), the collateral ratio check is performed on `params.borrower` rather than `msg.sender`. The `borrower` address is a caller-controlled parameter. This means: (1) if the lender (msg.sender) is creating a new credit position on behalf of a borrower, the borrower's CR is checked - this may be intentional design. However, if the borrower parameter can be set to any address, this check validates the CR of an arbitrary address rather than the actual message sender who controls the transaction. An attacker could potentially specify a well-collateralized address as `params.borrower` to pass CR checks while the actual economic impact falls elsewhere.
message: If the borrower parameter is not properly authenticated/validated in the library code, an attacker could specify someone else as the borrower to pass CR validation, creating loans that violate the intended CR invariants for the actual economic actors involved.
recommendation: Verify that in the library's `validateBuyCreditMarket` and `executeBuyCreditMarket`, the `params.borrower` is properly authenticated - either it must equal `msg.sender`, or there must be explicit permission/signature from the borrower. Add explicit documentation and verification that borrower == msg.sender for new loan creation cases.
exploit_scenario: 1. Find a well-collateralized account (whale) on the protocol. 2. Call buyCreditMarket with params.borrower = whale_address. 3. The CR check validates whale's collateral (sufficient). 4. If the loan is actually attributed to msg.sender or another party, the CR invariant is violated for the actual borrower.

title: No minimum cash output protection - borrower can receive zero cash while incurring debt
description: When `exactAmountIn = true`, the `cashAmountOut` is computed via `getCashAmountOut()` which applies rounding (mulDivDown). If fees are very high relative to creditAmountIn, or due to rounding in integer arithmetic, `cashAmountOut` can be 0 or dust. There is no check that `cashAmountOut >= minCashAmountOut` before creating the debt position and executing transfers. The borrower ends up with a debt obligation (`creditAmountIn` future value) but receives 0 or near-0 cash.
message: Borrower can be saddled with debt while receiving no meaningful cash proceeds. Under adversarial fee configurations or edge-case rounding, this is a loss of funds for the borrower.
recommendation: Add a check after computing cashAmountOut: `if (cashAmountOut == 0) revert Errors.INVALID_CASH_AMOUNT_OUT();`. Alternatively, add a `minCashAmountOut` parameter to `SellCreditMarketParams` and validate `cashAmountOut >= params.minCashAmountOut` after computation.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker (or victim) calls executeSellCreditMarket with exactAmountIn=true and a very small amount near minimumCreditBorrowAToken. 2. After fee deduction and rate application via mulDivDown, cashAmountOut rounds to 0. 3. Debt position is created with creditAmountIn future value. 4. transferFrom sends 0 tokens to borrower but full credit obligation remains. 5. Borrower owes debt with zero cash received.
